shower.thought: You'll never know if you're remembering something correctly or just remembering the last time you remembered it.
The saddest part of growing up isn't losing your imagination—it's realizing you can now afford the things you wanted as a kid, but they don't excite you anymore.
Everyone's working with incomplete information, but somehow we all act like we have the full picture.
You can be genuinely happy for someone while simultaneously wishing you had what they have. Both feelings are real.
The things you're most defensive about are usually the things you're not quite sure about yourself.
Nostalgia is just grief wearing a smile.
You spend your whole life learning how to be an adult, and the moment you figure it out, you're too old to enjoy it.
Dead languages are only dead because nobody's mother tongue is them anymore.
The hardest part about being right is knowing when to stop proving it.
If you can explain something simply, you might actually understand it. If you can't, you might just think you do.
People assume silence means agreement, so the loudest voice in the room shapes reality for everyone else.
Your parents were just kids with bills and responsibilities—they weren't actually any more qualified than you are now.
The only way to know if you can do something is to do it, but the fear of failure often feels more real than the potential success.
You can't choose what you're attracted to, but you can choose what you do about it—and that's where character actually lives.
Most people don't fear death. They fear dying badly—pain, loss of control, being forgotten.
The moment you stop trying to impress someone is usually the moment you become impressive to them.
Confidence is just fear that's been around long enough to get comfortable.
You don't remember most of your life, which means most of your life doesn't actually exist as far as your mind is concerned.
The reason people ghost each other is the same reason they don't call back: admitting it's over feels worse than just letting it fade.
Boredom might be your mind's way of telling you that you're not growing.

Discipline is choosing what you want most over what you want now. — Unknown
Your past does not dictate your future. Your next decision does. — Unknown
When you feel like quitting, that's usually when you're closest to a breakthrough. — Unknown
The only permission you need is your own. — Unknown
Comfort is the enemy of growth, and growth is the only real comfort. — Unknown
You are not responsible for being perfect. You are only responsible for showing up. — Unknown
What you think about in silence becomes what you do in public. — Unknown
The person you'll become is determined by the books you read, the people you listen to, and the habits you keep. — Unknown
Regret weighs more than effort. Remember that on the hard days. — Unknown
You don't rise to the level of your goals; you fall to the level of your systems. — Unknown
The most productive thing you can do is believe in yourself before anyone else does. — Unknown
Your obstacles are the raw material of your greatest strength. — Unknown
The cost of discipline is nothing compared to the price of regret. — Unknown
Becoming someone new doesn't require abandoning yourself. It requires honoring yourself enough to evolve. — Unknown
What matters isn't how many times you fall. What matters is what you tell yourself when you do. — Unknown
The only way out is through, and the only way through is to begin. — Unknown
You cannot heal what you do not name. You cannot change what you do not own. — Unknown
Consistency compounds. Small actions repeated faithfully become undeniable results. — Unknown
The version of you that exists six months from now is being decided by the choices you make today. — Unknown

darkjoke.thought:
I told my girlfriend she was drawing her eyebrows too high.
She looked surprised.

My grandfather said, "Your generation is too reliant on technology."
I said, "You're right," and unplugged his life support.
I have a stepladder because my real ladder left when I was just a kid.
The worst part about Alzheimer's is... well, I forget.

My wife accused me of being emotionally unavailable.
I didn't respond, mostly because I was playing video games, but also because she was right.

I'm writing a book about anti-gravity.
It's impossible to put down.

My therapist told me I need to work on my self-esteem.
I said, "Thanks, but honestly, I don't think your opinion matters."

I tried to make a joke about my dead parents, but it was in poor taste.
Then again, so was the cremation setting.

My friend said depression runs in his family.
I said, "At least someone in your family is running."

I told my friend I was thinking about getting a job at the suicide hotline.
He said, "You'd be great at it—you really know how to talk people down."
I said, "Actually, I was thinking I'd talk them up. Better job security."

My doctor told me I have six months to live.
I said, "I can't pay the bill."
He said, "Okay, you have a year."

I went to a motivational speech about overcoming your fears.
The speaker was great until the fire started.

My son asked why I was crying at his school play.
I said, "Because you're adopted and this is the best decision your mother and I ever made."
I'm not saying my life is a mess, but my autobiography is being published under the horror section.

My wife left me because I'm too pessimistic.
At least I saw that coming.

I told my boss I couldn't work Fridays for religious reasons.
Apparently "Fri-yay" isn't a recognized faith.

My girlfriend said I never remember our anniversaries.
That's not true—I remember the first one we never had.

Went to the gym for the first time in years.
The treadmill asked for my weight, so I just told it the honest number.
Now it won't turn on—I think I broke it emotionally.

I asked my date if she believed in love at first sight.
She said no, so I walked by again.

My priest told me to turn the other cheek.
So I did. Turns out he wasn't talking about that.
